To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) dEVI derived with Quickbird data had a slightly higher correlation with burn severity than dNBR derived with Landsat TM data, 2) dNBR derived using ASTER had a similar correlation to dNBR derived by Landsat TM data and 3) MODIS data were not correlated with ground data.
the dEVI and dNBR derived using the ASTER sensor were the best performing indices for detecting burn severity, with dEVI showing slightly better results.

the differenced EnhancedVegetationIndex derived from the QuickBird and the differenced normalised burn ratio derived from the ASTER were the most accurate methods for detecting burn severity, followed by the differenced normalized burn ratio derived from Landsat TM data.

the ASTER-derived dNBR and Quickbird-derived dEVI were the most accurate sensors for estimating burn severity in this study.
the dNBR and dEVI are both good predictors of burn severity in ponderosapine forests, and that the dEVI from Quickbird and dNBR from ASTER were slightly better than the dNBR from Landsat.
The relatively coarser resolution MODIS-derived NDVI image was weakly correlated with ground data (R2 = 0.38).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that the best sensor to use for measuring burn severity in ponderosas is ASTER.
ASTER and QuickBird are the most promising sensors for burn severity assessment.
the dNBR and dEVI derived for ASTER, Quickbird and Landsat data are all good candidates for measuring burn severity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ASTER data are an effective alternative to Landsat data for characterising burn severity.
the ASTER-derived dNBR and the Quickbird-derived dEVI were comparable to the Landsat-derived dNBR in terms of the strength of the correlation between field data and satellite data.
ASTER and Quickbird data provide a viable alternative to Landsat data for mapping post-fire burn severity.
